Ahasbai
ah-HAS-bye
n. (father of Eliphelet, one of David's thirty; also called Ur, named twice)
Hebrew 'Achasbai, of uncertain sense; the translators' margin at 1 Chronicles 11:35 gives Ahasbai as an alternative to Ur, so that one man bears both names.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Ahasbai is named as a father in the roll of the thirty: “Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite” (2 Samuel 23:34). The Chronicles parallel names the same man's son differently and his father differently again: “Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur” (1 Chronicles 11:35) — and the translators' margin at that verse notes Eliphal as an alternative for Eliphelet and Ur as an alternative for Ahasbai. One man, then, under two names, which is common enough in Israel; this entry covers both and no separate entry is made for Ur. He is called the son of the Maachathite, which places the family on the northern border toward Maachah. The company he belonged to is set out in the surrounding verses: “Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Hararite” (2 Samuel 23:33), and the whole is counted at the end: “Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all” (2 Samuel 23:39). A father named twice, each time under a different name, with nothing recorded of him but that his son stood with David.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828): Ahasbai, the father of Eliphelet, one of David's thirty; the same man is called Ur in Chronicles.

Hebrew 'Achasbai, of uncertain derivation.

He was the father of Eliphelet, one of David's thirty.

He is called the son of the Maachathite, 2 Samuel 23:34.

The margin at 1 Chronicles 11:35 gives Ahasbai for Ur.

The same verse gives Eliphal for Eliphelet.

Key Scripture

2Sa 23:34 — "Eliphelet the son of Ahasbai, the son of the Maachathite, Eliam the son of Ahithophel the Gilonite,"

1Ch 11:35 — "Ahiam the son of Sacar the Hararite, Eliphal the son of Ur,"

2Sa 23:33 — "Shammah the Hararite, Ahiam the son of Sharar the Hararite,"

2Sa 23:39 — "Uriah the Hittite: thirty and seven in all."

Modern Corruption

Double names in the parallel rolls are offered as proof of textual confusion, where the translators' own margin shows the two names belong to one man.

expand to see more

Ahasbai and Ur, Eliphelet and Eliphal, Sharar and Sacar: four names for two men in two verses, and the whole cluster is regularly produced as evidence that the text has broken down. The Authorized Version's margin answers it on the page. The translators noted the alternatives at 1 Chronicles 11:35 precisely because they understood the names to be variants of one another, and they printed both rather than choosing. Men of Scripture commonly bore two names — Jacob and Israel, Simon and Peter, Saul and Paul — and a register is not corrupt for recording the one its own source used.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the one-entity rule is a rule of truth and not of tidiness. Ur and Ahasbai are one man, so he gets one entry and both names are named in it. A reference work that made two men out of two names would be adding to Scripture, not serving it.
